proposals.before: Year two opens with Ouyang Xiu’s note: in the Five Dynasties’ chaos five heirs took throne, yet four broke ancient practice on era names. Liang’s last emperor and Jin’s deposed emperor waited more than a year; Han’s Hidden Emperor and Zhou’s Shizong kept prior reign titles for life. The annals do not rebuke them—they record facts, and the fault is plain.
proposals.after: In the second year: in the chaotic age of the Five Dynasties, five successors took the throne, yet four did not change the reign title according to ancient practice. Liang’s last emperor and Jin’s deposed emperor, more than a year after accession, ought to have changed the era name but did not, changing only the following year. Han’s Hidden Emperor and Zhou’s Shizong both kept their predecessors’ era names to the end without change, and the annals offer no censure—they simply record the facts, and the fault shows itself.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic invents “Ouyang Xiu’s note” and framing absent from the Chinese; align with the literal historical comment.

proposals.before: Cold Food sacrifices in the open with spirit money burned, a new reign title proclaimed amid mourning while music played, Ma Yanji and Ren Yuan put to death—ritual, music, punishments, and policy were all but destroyed.
proposals.after: Cold Food sacrifices in the open with spirit money burned, a new reign title proclaimed amid mourning while music played, Ma Yan and Ren Yuan put to death—ritual, music, punishments, and policy were all but destroyed.
proposals.reason: Chinese 马延 is Ma Yan; “及” means “and” before 任圜, not part of the personal name.

proposals.before: On gengyin younger brothers Xi Rang were enfeoffed as Prince of Cao, Xi Jin as Prince of Ji, and Xi Hui as Prince of Qi.
proposals.after: On gengyin younger brother Xi Rang was enfeoffed as Prince of Cao, Xi Jin as Prince of Ji, and Xi Hui as Prince of Qi.
proposals.reason: Literal grammar error: “younger brothers Xi Rang were” should treat Xi Rang as singular subject of the first enfeoffment.
